prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall state and Z2 topological insulators, and for the first experimental realisation of the quantum spin Hall state in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: After the full first round I keep topological insulators as a single-part prize with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. The discovery is a phenomenon first: a bulk band topology that forces protected edge states, a new class of quantum matter. It has a short chain from prediction (2005) to first observation (2007), and about two decades of independent confirmation by transport, ARPES, STM and imaging in many materials. This is the most mature of the three leading candidates, and it is the only one of them where the central claim is neither an instrument advance (B034) nor still waiting for its mechanism (B046). My round-1 move from Hasan to Mele holds: the Z2 invariant and the quantum spin Hall proposal are one joint piece of work, and Johansson, Olsson, Lindroth and Mehlig all object to separating the pair. I would accept a citation worded narrowly as the 2D prediction plus first realisation, and I would state in the committee text that the three-dimensional branch and the HgTe proposal exist as context.
statement.case_against: The weakness is allocation, and I do not think the round has removed it. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed HgTe, and Fu, Moore and Balents together with Kane and Mele opened the 3D branch, where Hasan did the decisive ARPES work. No trio from the supplied names covers all of this, so any B028 prize understates part of the field and must be worded to avoid claiming the whole discovery. The 2016 prize for topological phases and phase transitions is a legitimate reason for some members to wait, even though I read it as a different result (phase transitions and Hall precursors, not Z2 classification and protected edge and surface states). If the committee decides the credit would misstate the original work, B034 is the fallback I can defend.

responses.point: Johansson would accept Hasan only if the committee wants the citation to cover the 3D branch, at the cost of a theory slot, and otherwise prefers the compact prediction-plus-first-realisation prize.
responses.response: I agree with the structure of your argument and have moved to it. The 3D branch has a strong claim, but covering it properly needs Fu, Moore and Balents as well as Hasan, and three slots cannot do that. A narrow citation to the 2D prediction and first realisation is honest about what it recognises, while a citation that mentions 3D but credits only one of its contributors would be less accurate. I therefore drop my opening proposal of Hasan as my preferred configuration. Where I would still press is on wording: the citation should not say or imply that the whole field of topological insulators is credited to these three.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the 2016 topological-phases prize overlap is more significant than I suggested, and prefers B034 for its clean two-name credit and absence of overlap, with B028 as her first alternative.
responses.response: I take the overlap seriously, but I read the record differently. The 2016 prize honoured topological phase transitions and the quantum Hall precursors; it did not name the Z2 classification of time-reversal-invariant insulators or the protected helical edge states, and nothing in it predicts the HgTe experiment. B034 has a different overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes, in the sense that the clock builds on tools those prizes recognised. I accept your point that clean attribution is a real virtue, and it is why B034 is my first alternative. But a clean credit does not make a discovery larger, and I weigh the new phenomenon above the tidier list. I would change my view if the committee treated the 2016 overlap as decisive.

responses.point: Mehlig accepts the maturity and idea-to-observation chain for B028 as his fallback, but argues that its allocation problem is worse than that of B046, whose theory-plus-experiment pair is cleaner, and that adding Hasan would not solve it.
responses.response: I agree that Hasan does not solve the allocation problem, and I no longer propose him for that reason. I do not agree that B046 is cleaner. MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero are a clean core, but the third slot is open between Bistritzer and Andrei, Cao is outside the names, the pairing mechanism is unresolved, and the experiments are about eight years old. B028 has one hard decision (the third name) but a more settled body of evidence. If I had to decide between an incomplete credit on a mature discovery and a credit that may have to be revised on an immature one, I would choose the former. I would be willing to look at B046 first next year if the committee does not decide for it now.

responses.point: Olsson names B034 as the cleaner configuration if the committee judges that the B028 credit misstates who is responsible for the original work, and stresses that Kane and Mele should not be split.
responses.response: I share your condition and your fallback. Kane and Mele stay together, and the committee should check that the citation does not read as crediting the whole subject to three people. If the committee decides that the omissions of Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu, Moore and Balents make B028 misleading, then B034 is the right step down for me, and I would then support it on its merits as an invention with a clean credit. I do not think the omissions reach that threshold when the citation names a specific prediction and a specific first realisation. I would value your view on whether your spectroscopy experience makes you more or less comfortable with a 2D-only citation.

responses.point: Pearce proposes B034 with B005 as a two-part prize and identifies the one-name Halzen credit as the weakest element, saying the astroparticle part falls away if it cannot be justified.
responses.response: Your own test already answers the question I raised in round 1. I ranked B005 second and I still think neutrino astronomy deserves recognition, but a one-name credit for a detector and analysis effort of hundreds, with AMANDA and the analysis leaders unnamed, is not a form I can support, and I cannot answer Kroll's question about who made the first statistically decisive observation from the supplied record. Source identification is also still developing. On two parts more generally, I see no need for a two-part prize here: it forces a trade against the three-name limit and weakens both halves. I would not join a B034 plus B005 prize, though I remain open to B005 later if a defensible credit emerges.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a citation limited to the 2D prediction and first realisation, with the HgTe proposal and the 3D branch left outside the credited contributions.
How much weight the 2016 topological-phases prize should carry; Lindroth and Mehlig treat it as a possible reason to wait and I do not.
Exact priority among the 2005-2008 theory and experiment papers, which I rely on recalled history for and cannot verify from the supplied record.
Whether the novelty and pending-redefinition questions on B034 would change if the committee heard stronger evidence about other lattice-clock groups.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile: none of my documented connections (David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet, the Uppsala theory group) is tied to any credited name on the shortlist. Kroll's disclosed Hall-laboratory link concerns B034 only; I would leave it to the committee to weigh through transparency. My own preferred configuration is B028, so this does not affect it.
